I have reason to ask the minister a question or two and while I know that under provocation he can become acidulous, he is at heart a kind hearted man. A gentleman who is very

interested in this question of the rehabilitation of prisoners has written to me expressing concern about the possibility that the present government may cut out all sentences between the length of six months and one year, and he has asked me to inquire what is intended in this respect; what would be the line of demarcation between the sentences of men and women sent to prison and those sent to jail.

This was discussed briefly this afternoon. Before I enter upon that subject, however, perhaps I should express my appreciation of the remarks which the hon. member has made with respect to the commissioner, to whose services I should like to pay my tribute. I should remind the committee that we amended the Penitentiary Act last year to permit of the extension of the term of the present commissioner. At this time, particularly when we are embarking upon this extensive program of reform and modernization, we consider it essential that we should retain his services as long as we are able to have the benefit of the experience of this highly qualified and dedicated officer.
With respect to the question of the difference between the six months and one year terms, I will just be brief, because, as I say, we discussed this this afternoon. The hon. member will recollect that the federal government agreed to assume responsibility for all persons sentenced to terms of more than six months. This was agreed to in principle, and the provinces agreed to it in principle at the conference which was held last October. It is, however, our view that as we are increasingly placing the emphasis in our institutions upon reform and rehabilitation programs it would not be sensible to commit to these institutions prisoners who are given sentences of only six months, or seven or eight months. The reason is that when one takes into account the automatic remission of sentence and parole considerations which are applicable to reduce the length of a sentence at one end, and when one takes into account the length of time consumed by the classification and admission process at the other end, it works out that of a sentence of even 12 months to only about nine months are actually served in the institution, and that of these nine months as much as six weeks may be taken up by the classification and admission procedures. This means there would be only some seven and a half months available for the man to undergo rehabilitation and reform training, and it is not possible to do a great deal of good, in most cases, in that period.
It was therefore our view that at least the federal statutes should be amended so that no sentences might be imposed between six months and one year, and magistrates and
Supply-J ustice
judges would be asked to consider in their sentencing practices that if only a short sentence is required by way of what one might call a mild retributive punishment a sentence of six months or less would probably be adequate, coupled with, or as an alternative to, a fine, but if that what a man needs is a reform and training program leading to his rehabilitation a sentence of less than 12 months would scarcely permit such a program to be started before the man was due for release, and that therefore it is not sensible to send a man to a federal institution for a period of less than 12 months. That is the thought behind it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Order. I believe that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has been answered by the Minister of Justice who says this matter does not come under his jurisdiction and, as it does not, therefore it is not relevant to the item before us.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to see that the minister is not a hangman. Under this item I should like to pursue what I dealt with in my earlier remarks under item 150. Item 159 covers grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies. The amount this year is $75,000 compared with $60,000 last year. My question is this. Are these the same societies previously mentioned by the minister under item 150?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are proposing to pay this year $75,000 to recognized prisoners' aid societies. The amount this year last year. There is an increase under this item of $15,000 and an increase under the departmental item which we discussed earlier of $10,000 representing a total increase of $25,000. The organizations to which these grants are paid under the penitentiaries vote are as follows: The John Howard Society of British Columbia, the John Howard Society of Vancouver Island, the John Howard Society of Alberta, the John Howard Society of Saskatchewan, the John Howard Society and Elizabeth Fry Society of Manitoba, the John Howard Society of Ontario, La Society d'Orientation et de Rehabilitation de Montreal, Le Service de Readaptation Sociale de Quebec, the Catholic Rehabilitation Service of Montreal, the John Howard Society of New Brunswick, the John Howard Society of Nova Scotia, the John Howard Society of St. John's, Newfoundland, the Salvation Army Prison Aid Service, the Elizabeth Fry Society of Kingston and the John Howard Society of Quebec.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am certainly not going to ask the minister for his views on capital punishment but there is one question I should like to ask. It is my understanding that the government of Saskatchewan has informed the minister that in the future it will not permit capital punishment to be exercised in provincial institutions there. If that is correct, what is the decision of the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: minister concerning the use of penitentiaries as such? Is Saskatchewan to be a province where you can feel pretty safe concerning the commutation of sentences?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am really unable to answer that question because the case has not arisen and, as I suggested already, the question of capital punishment has no relevancy to the item on penitentiaries we are now discussing.

Mr. Chairman, when the minister answered my earlier remarks I failed to hear him deal with one question I asked. At the present time prisoners are allowed to write four letters a month to relatives. Would the minister give consideration to permitting them to write more?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I certainly could undertake to review that question. We would have to see what the implications might be with respect to staff. I can assure my hon. friend that we have a number of staff problems at the moment and I say that without trying to minimize the human relationship of the problem he has referred to. All I can undertake to do is to have a look at it without at this time being able to make a firm commitment about what we could do.
I do not think this point arose in discussion between the minister and myself but it is my understanding that the length of visits of family or friends to inmates is restricted to one hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the maximum period that may be allowed.
What are the total number of hours a day during which visiting is permitted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, the time during which the prison is open in general is from 9.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m.
That would be-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Seven hours.
Seven hours a day, six days a week?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Five days a week.

Thirty-five hours a week;
therefore, he could have a maximum of 35 visits a week?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That would depend entirely on the size of the visiting rooms. The visiting rooms, as I am sure my hon. friend knows from his own visits and inspections of the penitentiaries, accommodate-the	visiting
rooms, I am told, accommodate from 10 to 20 visits simultaneously, each room being partitioned.
Supply-Justice

Perhaps I should have used the words "if only one person visited in a particular area". On a very rough guess, if there is a minimum of 10 visits a day, then you could allow 350 visits a week and I am sure that not all inmates undertake to have visits once a month. I am sure that many of them may have only one or two visits a year, depending on how far away the person's family is from the site of the penitentiary. But it would appear that the argument for not relaxing the number of visits per month has not too much of a base, if this is the case. For instance, I take the case of Kingston itself. Unless you had the visiting area full of its maximum number of inmates for every hour if all of the visits were allowed, then you would have a problem of not being able to relax or extend the visits. I am sure that is not the case. For instance, in Kingston there are many times when the visiting room is not full. I am sure there may be times when no one is visiting any of the inmates at all. The minister nods his head. I take that to mean that what I am saying is substantially correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but our difficulty is that we have to take account of the peak period. For instance, most visitors come in the afternoon between two and four. If we could insist humanely that visits be spread equally over all the day, then we could probably physically accommodate more than one visit a month; but we cannot compel or regiment the times at which relatives wish to visit an inmate. We therefore have to take account of the fact that there will be great peak periods. Unless we restrict the number of visits, you will find that some inmates cannot receive even as many as one visit a month because of the fact that visitors tend to come at peak times.

But you do restrict and regiment the number of times they can come during the month, and the hours of the day during which they can come and the length of time during which the visitor can remain on the premises? You restrict and regiment the facilities which exist in so far as the visit is concerned. I understand there must be certain restrictions and certain requirements with respect to the visitors because of the fear that some weapon may be passed to the inmate. We do know there is a very close watch kept on the physical contact between the inmate and his wife, or vice versa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We do not write to a proposed visitor or prospective visitor and say you may come only between, let us say, nine and ten in the morning on such and such a day. We do endeavour so far as possible to allow the visits to take place when the visitors wish

Supply-Justice
to come. They will be in touch with the institution and with the inmates and will do their best to arrange a time which is convenient to them, and we try to accommodate them at that time. We find that in order to accommodate visitors we have to take account of the fact that there are peak periods. We have not yet been able to devise a system of more than one visit a month, but when our accommodation problem is lessened we shall be able to have another look at that.

I was not suggesting that you write to the prospective visitor and say, "You have to be here at two o'clock" or anything of that nature, but you do restrict the period of time within the day during which a visit can take place, and that is between nine and four o'clock. That is the restriction I was talking about. What I was leading up to was this. Even though your peak periods may be in the afternoon and your slack periods may be in the morning, I think you could make some arrangement and allow this even if it is on a special basis. There will be special problems with respect to visiting facilities, and the inmate overcrowding problem is such that you are not able to say: "We will allow two visits a month". You could not cope with that. I am sure you could, even under those crowded conditions, make special arrangements in particular cases between the inmate and his relative so that the relative who wanted to come to visit could do so. You could then arrange a satisfactory time which might be in the morning in so far as the extra visit is concerned. I am quite sure that could be done without too much difficulty, and you would not then, as you say, be entering into the field of regimenting visitors and say that they have to come at a certain hour. You could work it out in a mutually satisfactory way so far as a visit beyond the normal one visit per month is concerned. I hope that some arrangement along these lines can be made for inmates who desire to have or are able to have more than one visitor per month.
I would also suggest and also think that the number of letters that an inmate is permitted to write to relatives may be extended to people who may be close friends but are not relatives. That could be given consideration also. The question of more relaxed circumstances as between the relationship of the visitor and the person he is visiting could be looked into and some arrangements made along that line similar to that which exists in the institution at Chino, California, where there is a very relaxed, informal, almost picnic arrangement between the inmate and his wife and children who come to visit him. I am quite sure if we could

move into the direction of relaxing the rigidity of restrictions and the rules that apply to physical contact between the inmate and the person who came to visit him, along with additional letters, you might assist somewhat in hastening the rehabilitating and reforming process of the inmate and make him feel perhaps a little more accepted and less fit and less upset by his incarceration and all the things that surround him. I hope the minister will be able to move in this direction as quickly as possible and allow more letters and more relaxed conditions in so far as visits are concerned. So far as is humanely possible, he should relax the limit of one visit per month for one hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; I realize to some extent that we perhaps have been talking at cross purposes, because I have been discussing the rule of general application. Because of the accommodation problems and the physical condition of the majority of the buildings which we have, I am bound to think of institutions such as Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul. My hon. friend says he hopes we will move in this direction. I should like him to go and look at the William Head and Valley-field institutions. These are new institutions. If he does that he will see that exactly what he has been talking is being followed in these institutions. The conditions and atmosphere there are much more relaxed, with minimum security and the men have relatively much more freedom to move about as they will. These, as I point out, are experimental stations. This is the type of new institution toward which we want to move and which it is our intention to bring about. In what I have been saying previously I have been thinking of the present circumstances under which we have to operate in the majority of our institutions.
I regret intruding into this conversation. I wonder whether I can ask the minister what is the average cost to maintain a prisoner for one year in federal penal institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The average cost for everything-I am having some arithmetic done- including salaries of staff was $5.66 a day. I am having some arithmetic done to arrive at the annual figure.
While the minister is working on his arithmetic-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It appears to be $2,064.42 according to the latest figure we have.
When there is commutation of a sentence of hanging and it is changed to life imprisonment, what would the average period of time be in years before the prisoner would be paroled?

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My answer has to be that there is no average period. It would depend entirely on each case and the reports that were made by the prison authorities, and from now on it will depend on the decision made by the national parole board based on their review of the case.

Could the minister perhaps indicate the range, for example, the smallest number of years and the maximum number of years? I am trying to get a rough indication. I do not want to try to pin the minister down but simply to get a rough idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I regret that the penitentiaries branch does not have these statistics. The remission service or the new parole board, which items have been passed, would have had these figures.

I should like to ask one more question. I went at the matter backwards and I seem to be having more success this way. With respect to the penitentiaries already in existence, is any consideration being given to establishing a central execution chamber using either gas or electricity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have already explained and am sorry to have to repeat that it is not part of the authority or responsibility of the federal penitentiaries system to carry out executions and I am unable to answer that question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair has already ruled on that matter.
I should like to ask the minister if any consideration has ever been given to trying to make prisoners self-supporting?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To what?
To make prisoners self-supporting so they can earn their keep in the same way as those who live outside prison walls.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Prisoners who work in the prisons are paid a daily amount for their work but I will not pretend for a moment that it actually enables them to be selfsupporting. I might point out to the committee that one of the reforms made this year which the penitentiaries branch has been quite anxious to see brought about is incorporated in the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which were given third reading today whereby an inmate who was entitled to unemployment insurance benefits at the time of his com-mital to penitentiary no longer automatically forfeits those benefits by virtue of time spent in prison. Therefore, in a number of cases, and we hope an increasingly large
Supply-Justice
number, a discharged inmate will be entitled to receive unemployment insurance benefits until such time as he becomes reestablished in employment. We feel that will be a forward step in assisting released or paroled inmates to re-establish themselves in civil life.
I should like to ask the minister how many penitentiaries there are under his jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are just trying to figure out the ones under construction. Those now in operation number nine and two satellites. There are two under construction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can the minister tell me how many prisoners are now in penitentiaries whose capital sentences have been commuted in the last two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the question had been raised under the remission service item I could have given the answer straight away but we do not have it here in that form for the last two years. It will be necessary to find out how many cases have been commuted in the last two years and then I could answer.
There is one question I should like to ask. Did the figure which the minister gave for board and lodging include clothing and depreciation and overhead so far as the buildings are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed it includes all clothing but no depreciation.
It does include the salaries of the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

I should like to express one thought with respect to the general import of the question asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I hope he was not trying to place a dollar value on human lives in the question he asked.

Mr. Chairman, surely this is outrageously out of order. If the hon. member was not allowed to ask his question it is an outrage for some other hon. member to be allowed to get up and make comments on the question he was not allowed to ask.
My friend is probably just becoming impatient for one of the following items to be reached.
I just like to see a little justice around here.
My friend, coming from the province he does and talking about justice-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order.

Supply-Justice
I hope the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond was not trying to establish that we should place a dollar value on human lives and determine whether it is cheaper-
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is making reference to capital punishment.
No, I am not making reference to capital punishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The earlier observation was with reference to capital punishment and I submit that the discussion is out of order.

One question asked related to the cost of keeping an inmate in a penitentiary and how long he might stay there if his sentence had been commuted to life imprisonment. I assume the follow-up is to connect that with what might have happened to the person who is an inmate. I regret that this question was not raised under another item so that we could have cleared it up completely. Perhaps it is a case of misunderstanding on my part but it did raise that question in my mind. I am not trying to say that is what the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond meant or implied or said but it did raise that question in my mind. I regret that the hon. member is not here now to clear up that question.
I am sure he did not mean that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
160. Operation and maintenance of penitentiaries, Including supplies and services relating thereto: administration, operation, repair and upkeep of buildings, works and equipment; maintenance, discharge and transfer of inmates: compensation to discharged inmates permanently disabled while in penitentiaries, $12,705,059.

I should like to ask the
minister what the reason is for the very marked reduction as shown in the details in the cost of operation and maintenance in the province of Newfoundland. Is it that there are so many fewer prisoners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am happy to be able to advise my hon. friend that the number of prisoners maintained in Newfoundland has gone down from over 40 to 29.
What is done with female prisoners in Newfoundland? Are there any?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are none at the present time under our jurisdiction with sentences of two years or more, and I do not know whether there are any under provincial responsibility.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
In the rather unusual circumstances in which there would be a female prisoner sentenced to two years or more, what would happen? I think that is largely a hypothetical question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that there are some accommodations under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities in Newfoundland for female prisoners and under the arrangement we have with the government of Newfoundland female prisoners would stay in Newfoundland and be looked after by the provincial authorities to whom we would pay compensation.

Can the minister say what these arrangements are and where that place is because at one stage I had something to do with some negotiations with respect to getting a building for women prisoners? At that time, on the rare occasion when a woman was sentenced in Newfoundland, they had no place in which to confine her and they just let her go. The provincial authorities were trying to find some place for women prisoners. I was genuinely interested in finding out whether anything had happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not had any indications from or discussions with the Newfoundland authorities on that question. I do not recall that the attorney general raised it when we had our conference last October. We had a very general discussion regarding the arrangements in effect between us, but it was my understanding that Newfoundland was quite satisfied with the present arrangements. I am informed that they have some arrangement in the prison at St. John's for accommodating women prisoners. I am not aware that they are not satisfied, and I have had no complaints.
There are no federal women prisoners in Newfoundland at all, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: None at the moment.
Are all of those male prisoners who were sentenced to over two years kept in the penitentiary in N ewf oundland ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand they are either in the prison at St. John's or the camp at Salmonier.
Can the minister say what amount is paid to the province for the custody of each of these prisoners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is $5.60 per day; that is the price at which other prisoners are maintained. I understand it is six cents below the price paid-
Six cents below?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is six cents below the price paid elsewhere.
Nothing is paid for rent because the minister has just told us-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is just the cost.
In other words, these people are being kept by the province of Newfoundland rent free.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I don't know what my hon. friend means by rent free. It includes all the cost of what would otherwise be described as board, lodging, clothing, staff salaries, and so on.

Perhaps the minister did not understand the purport of my earlier question. I asked him if that item that was mentioned included any allowance for overhead or building depreciation, and he said no. Now, he has just told us it costs $5.60-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is heat and so on; that would be a rent factor.

I am not talking about heat and light; I do not regard them as rent. It costs $5.66 a day per head, and actually Newfoundland is only paid $5.60. The $5.66 includes no amount for accommodation and, as I said, therefore it would appear that these prisoners are being kept by the government of Newfoundland rent free.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This rate has been revised from time to time, and this is the arrangement which has been in effect for many years. I am sorry it has taken my hon. friend this long to find out about it. I am surprised that he should only become exercised about it after there has been a change of government.
I am not in the least exercised about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You seem to be quite concerned.

I imagine before the inflation, for which the hon. gentleman's colleague is responsible, that cost on the mainland was probably about $5.25 per day in which circumstance the $5.60 would probably have included some little allowance for rental.
There was one other point about which I wanted to ask the minister. Is there a long term agreement with the government of Newfoundland or what is the nature of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed it is a written agreement, approved by order in council here and in Newfoundland, and it has effect until some other arrangement is agreed upon by the two governments.

Has the government any thought of bringing this arrangement to an
Supply-Justice
end and looking after prisoners in the way in which they are looked after in all the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will be looking into that when we get the over-all report from the correctional planning committee, with recommendations for a long term building program for federal penal institutions in Canada. There is no thought of a revision at the present time, and we are not being pressed in that direction at all by the government of Newfoundland.

I have a couple of questions for the minister on this item. In recent months I have noticed quite a lot of advertisements for instructors for the penal staff, particularly at the Dorchester institution. I wonder if the minister could indicate to the committee if this staff will, in any way, be associated with training new men for the proposed institution at Springhill and, secondly, if the commissioner and the minister will give the senior employees at Dorchester, those who have given long years of service to his department, at least a fair opportunity of getting some of the senior positions in the new institution?
Another point I should like to mention concerns housing for those presently employed at Dorchester.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps I could answer these two questions asked so far, because the answer to both questions is yes.

That more or less takes the questions out of my mind, Mr. Chairman. I thank the minister for his interest in the matter. I hope that if he comes to Dorchester in the immediate future he will not only inspect the institution but will also take an interest in the housing accommodation, which I must admit is no credit to his department.

I note that according to pages 227 and 228 in the blue book there is an increase of 150 in the number of personnel under this item. Is the committee to understand that the reason for that increase is the same as that which the minister gave when we started discussing the first item of penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This item results very largely from the necessity of providing staff for Joyceville, which, as I stated, will be coming into operation this fall, as well as the necessity for providing staff for the increased prison population at other institutions. Then, there are certain specialists whom we are recruiting in so far as we are able to find persons with the proper qualifications.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Justice
161. Construction, improvements and equipment, $6,058,571.
I wonder if the minister could tell us precisely what buildings are being constructed at the present time? There is a list on page 230, but it is not very illuminating.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the list of the actual number of buildings under construction is very extensive. I would be prepared to provide it if my hon. friend wishes it, but I wonder if he does not wish to know at what points major construction is taking place?
Perhaps the first question I should ask the minister is, does the department pay for these small buildings that are constructed to house the small detachments of police in many parts of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend would have to wait for that information until we reach the Royal Canadian Mounted Police item. This relates only to penitentiary construction.
I would be quite interested in knowing how many buildings have been started since the minister became minister, if he could list those-that is major projects, and where they are?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At St. Vincent de Paul we are building a new institution which, as I said, is very much along the lines of the one still under construction at Joyceville, and also at St. Vincent de Paul there is a major dormitory building which will be able to accommodate 104 inmates. At Valleyfield we have taken over and are in the process of renovating and altering an army camp there as a satellite institution for St. Vincent de Paul. At William Head, there was the takeover, remodelling and alteration of the old quarantine buildings formerly occupied or owned or at least administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. In addition to that, there is a sizeable dormitory building within the present area of the Prince Albert penitentiary accommodating some sixty inmates. Then there was the conversion of a building at Stony Mountain to provide dormitory accommodation for some fifty inmates, as I recall it. There was the complete new kitchen building in the existing institution at Kingston penitentiary; a large dairy barn at Collins Bay; a new piggery building for the farm at Dorchester, $20,000; a new shop building at Manitoba penitentiary, eventually $60,000, $20,000 in this year's estimates; a warehouse building in British Columbia, total cost about $30,000, $15,000 in this year's estimates. That is the type of building. There are three of what I might call major new

institutions or satellite institutions. St. Vincent de Paul, William Head, Valleyfield, and Springhill definitely will be available this year by way of new or satellite institutions. There are other buildings of the type I have detailed which are by way of addition or alteration to existing institutions.
There are a few questions I should like to ask about some of these matters. Perhaps the minister would like to answer them as we go along.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend is asking a question he might follow the usual custom of rising in his place.

I should be glad to do so. I am so accustomed to being in these numerous committees in other parts of the building where we do not have to stand up-in fact, if we do so, we never get a chance to speak- that I failed to do so in this instance. At St. Vincent de Paul there is a complete new institution. Can the minister tell me what the department's estimate was of the cost of these buildings, what the successful tender was and whether there was a single tender for the whole institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The departmental estimate of the total cost is, I am advised, approximately $5 million. There was provided in last year's estimates $800,000 and there is provided in this year's main estimates $3,340,000. It is not feasible to build institutions of this type under one general contract or to have all phases of construction proceeding at the same time. Therefore there are a number of individual contracts let, in some cases for individual sections of the building and in other cases for the installation of the general heating plant after the building is erected and also for equipment and so on to operate the machine shops and so on. Hence, there will be a series of individual contracts.
Can the minister give the committee a list of these contracts and the dates on which they were awarded?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to have a list compiled and to furnish it before the conclusion of the discussion of my estimates.

I should like to have some information with respect to the dormitory at St. Vincent de Paul. The Valleyfield business, of course, is just reconstruction and I should be quite satisfied if we could have the departmental estimate of the total amount of the contracts and the same for William Head and for Prince Albert. In every case I should like to know whether there was just one contract or whether there were several contracts and what the reason was in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, a fair proportion of this building is being done by our own inmate labour.

Of course, the minister can indicate that fact also. We have been told in another place by experts in the field of public works-and this is, of course, as Your Honour will readily appreciate, the reason why I am asking these questions-that under proper procedures, with proper building methods, the complete plan is prepared and one contract is called from one contractor for the whole of the institution and that any other way of doing things is wasteful, extravagant and wrong. We had a good deal of testimony to that effect in another place in another session of parliament. It is therefore only natural that we should be interested in finding out whether these principles that were enunciated to us are being followed by the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friend will remember that on both sides of the house there was pressure-and it was proper pressure-to institute immediate programs of work. It was our objective, which we realized in accordance, to let contracts for the construction of these buildings just as soon as plans for any particular section could be prepared and brought to the position where a contract could be let. If my hon. friend is suggesting that we should have delayed-
Perhaps the hon. member will allow me to do my own suggesting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I have the floor now because the hon. member gave it to me.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is any suggestion that we should have delayed in the awarding of contracts and the providing of employment until the plans for the building of the whole thing were prepared I wish my hon. friend would say so. I think he will agree that would be inconsistent with the position formerly taken.

I have no intention of saying anything about that matter until I have the information so that I can formulate some view as to whether or not there is any prima facie case. There were arguments made, of course, in another place, in other circumstances, about another building of precisely the same character, and for precisely the same reasons that the hon. gentleman has given now. I should think that if they were valid in one case they would be valid in the other. But their validity can be determined only by an examination of
Supply-Justice
the facts and not by theory. That was, of course, the view that I took in another place. I am not making any suggestions or any insinuations. I am seeking information.
I think it would be desirable to have the same information about this conversion project at Stony Mountain which sounds as though it would be quite a large one; for the kitchen at Kingston; and for the dairy barn at Collin's Bay. I do not know about the piggery. Piggeries have an important place in the history of confederation, it is true. Perhaps it would be as well to have the information for the piggery also and for the warehouse in British Columbia. What I am seeking to point out is that here we are voting a considerable sum of money to let, as we are told, a number of contracts as soon as the plans can be drawn up in order to provide employment as quickly as possible. It is our duty here in the committee of supply to get all the information we can in order to make sure that the taxpayers' money is being spent to the best possible advantage. If we could have about all those projects information of the kind that I suggest, I think it would be very helpful to the committee.

speechtext: 1 have provided the information for which the hon. gentleman asked with regard to St. Vincent de Paul, though I have not been able to discover what use he is able to make of that information. That is plain nonsense.
The hon. member for Carle-ton is an expert in nonsense, plain and varnished.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish you would just give me a moment, Mr. Chairman. I well understand the reason for the hon. gentleman's outburst, but it is totally unjustified. I have not refused to obtain any information.
